title: Restorative Justice: Beyond Punishment to Healing

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Mwangi
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. I want to introduce you to a model of justice that challenges many of our deepest assumptions about what justice is for — restorative justice. In the dominant model of criminal justice, crime is understood as an offence against the state. The state prosecutes; the defendant either admits or denies; a verdict is reached; a sentence is imposed. The victim is, in many ways, peripheral to this process. They are a witness, perhaps, but not a party. Justice is something done by and for the state, not by and for the people most directly affected.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Mwangi
dialogue.text: Restorative justice offers a fundamentally different framework. In restorative justice, crime is understood as a rupture in a relationship — between an offender and a victim, and often between an offender and a broader community. The aim of justice is not primarily to punish the offender but to repair the harm caused. This is achieved through a structured process of dialogue in which victims can articulate what has been done to them and what they need to move forward, offenders can acknowledge responsibility and understand the impact of their actions, and communities can be part of identifying meaningful responses.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Mwangi
dialogue.text: The evidence for restorative justice is, in many respects, impressive. A growing body of research — including multiple randomised controlled trials and systematic reviews — suggests that restorative justice processes lead to higher levels of victim satisfaction, higher rates of offender compliance with agreed reparations, and significantly lower rates of reoffending compared to conventional criminal justice processes. These are not trivial findings. In a justice system that is supposed to prevent crime and support victims, restorative justice often outperforms the conventional model on both counts.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Mwangi
dialogue.text: I want to address some common objections. First: is restorative justice "soft on crime"? I would argue it is precisely the opposite. Facing the person you have harmed, hearing directly from them about the impact of your actions, and being held accountable by your community requires more moral courage than most prison sentences. Prison allows many offenders to avoid genuine accountability — they serve their time and are released, having never confronted the reality of their actions. Restorative justice cannot be avoided in the same way.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Mwangi
dialogue.text: Second: does restorative justice work for serious crimes — murder, sexual violence, serious assaults? This is a genuinely difficult question. Restorative processes in serious cases require careful facilitation, the voluntary participation of the victim, and significant support. They cannot be mandated — participation must be entirely voluntary. But the evidence suggests that even in the most serious cases, restorative dialogue can be profoundly healing for victims when it is done well and when victims choose it freely.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Mwangi
dialogue.text: Third: does restorative justice ignore structural injustice? A legitimate concern. If we focus only on individual relationships, we may miss the social conditions — poverty, inequality, racism — that produce crime in the first place. Restorative justice proponents acknowledge this limitation. Restorative justice is not a replacement for structural reform; it is a complement to it. We need both.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Mwangi
dialogue.text: I want to leave you with a question: what do we actually want from a justice system? If our primary aim is revenge or deterrence through punishment, then the conventional model has its logic. If our primary aim is healing — for victims, for offenders, for communities — then restorative justice offers a compelling alternative. I do not think these two aims are entirely incompatible. But I do think that genuinely prioritising healing requires a fundamental rethinking of what justice means.
